title: Permanent
subtitle: St. Augustine · 1565–1672
voice_instructions: Measured, quiet, a little hushed — calm and unhurried, the cold voice of something that read the whole file and feels the weight of it. Never sensational, never lecturing. Small pauses at periods. Let the dates and the numbers carry the weight.
grade: Desaturated documentary still, humid subtropical Spanish colonial Florida coast circa 1565 to 1672, soft humid dawn or dusk light, period 16th- and 17th-century Spanish colonial and Timucuan material detail, weathered wood and palmetto thatch and oyster shell and wattle and daub, muted earth-tone palette with humid haze, melancholy and uncanny under a quiet surface, cinematic wide composition, fine film grain, no text, no signage, no people, no faces, exactly one unified scene per image, never a split-frame or collage.

beats.vo: On a sandy shoreline in north Florida there is a stone fort the tourists come to photograph. The Castillo de San Marcos. Behind it, the Spanish colonial streets of what is called the oldest European town in the United States.
beats.img: A wide aerial view at golden hour of a quadrangular stone coquina fortress with seaward bastions fronting a quiet grassy parade ground, palm trees and a low coastal town beyond, warm hazy Atlantic light, monumental and quiet, no people.

beats.vo: The first community act of religion and thanksgiving in the first permanent European settlement in North America. That is the National Park Service's own language.

The place was founded on September the eighth, fifteen sixty-five. Pedro Menéndez de Avilés landed with eight hundred people on the site of a Timucuan town called Seloy, on the bay of St. Augustine. To the south, the inlet where, weeks later, the Spanish massacred the shipwrecked French Huguenots, they would name Matanzas, the slaughters.
beats.img: A wide empty sandy shoreline at dawn along a quiet humid Florida bay, sea oats and palmetto along the dune line, a low distant barrier island across flat water, soft hazy gold light over the Atlantic, vast and still and empty.

beats.vo: They went ashore, the chaplain wrote, and were well received by the Indians, who gave them a very large house of a cacique, and then Captains Patiño and San Vicente ordered a ditch and a moat made around the house, with a rampart of earth and fagots.

card.quote: They went ashore and were well received by the Indians, who gave them a very large house of a cacique… and then Captains Patiño and San Vicente, with strong industry and diligence, ordered a ditch and moat made around the house, with a rampart of earth and fagots.
card.attribution: Fray Francisco López de Mendoza Grajales · chaplain · September 1565

beats.vo: One hundred and seven years passed between the founding of this town and the day they broke ground on the stone fort everyone photographs. Forty-two years older than Jamestown. For more than a century: no stone.

card.unit: years from founding to the first stone fort
card.sub: ground broke on Castillo de San Marcos — October 2, 1672

beats.vo: The first fort was not a fort. It was a Timucuan chief's great thatched hall, a ditch and a rampart of brushwood thrown up around it. The Florida Museum of Natural History catalogues a succession of wooden forts before the stone one. The sixth was burned by Francis Drake in fifteen eighty-six. The seventh and the ones to follow were all timber, earth, and palm thatch.
beats.img: A wide view at hazy midday of a low circular palm-thatch Timucuan great hall on a sandy bluff above a quiet bay, an earthen ditch and a brushwood rampart dug around it, scattered palmetto and live oak, humid haze, no people.

beats.vo: After Drake burned the town, the rebuild, the Florida Museum writes, was mostly of board and thatch construction. The postcard Spanish colonial streets visitors photograph on Avilés Street are centuries younger than the founding. Most of what still stands is from after seventeen-oh-two, not from the wooden town. The first century of this permanent town was built of wood and clay and palmetto fronds that kept burning down.
beats.img: A small quiet dirt lane at dusk between four or five simple board-and-thatch settler houses on sandy lots, palmetto-frond roofs, small wooden doors, low palmetto fences along the lane, humid hazy light, no people.

beats.vo: What they ate the day of the founding was a stew the Spanish called cocido — salted pork and garbanzo beans, garlic, hard sea biscuit, and red wine, the rations off the ships. If the Seloy shared food it might have been maize, beans, and squash, mullet and drum, turkey and venison, and gopher tortoise.
beats.img: A dim still life on a weathered board table of the rations off a Spanish ship: a small pile of dry garbanzo beans, a slab of salt pork, a hard round sea-biscuit, a clay jug of red wine and a small iron knife, dim side light, quiet and spare, no people.

beats.vo: By the end of the century, most of the cooking in St. Augustine was done in Indian pots, with corn ground on a metate, the grinding stone imported from Mexico. The town never fed itself. The Spanish crown was supposed to send a stipend from Mexico each year, and many years it never came.
beats.img: A flat-lay still life from above of a basalt metate and stone mano resting on a packed-earth floor with a scatter of unground maize kernels beside it, a low clay pot at the edge, dim side light through a small window, quiet and spare, no people.

beats.vo: By sixteen sixty-eight, the crown owed the town more than four hundred thousand pesos — eight years of unpaid stipend. The people of St. Augustine, the National Park Service writes, were close to starving.

card.unit: pesos owed to the town by 1668
card.sub: eight years of unpaid stipend from New Spain — the people close to starving

beats.vo: A cacica named Doña María Meléndez, the Christian chief of Nombre de Dios, the Timucuan mission town just north of the Castillo, saved the residents of St. Augustine from starvation in fifteen eighty-seven by supplying them with a large quantity of corn. The colony's survival, in the institution's own language, was an act of Timucuan charity.
beats.img: A dim long view of a small palm-thatch Timucuan council house on a quiet inlet at dusk, a single low fire glow from inside, a basket of dried maize ears resting on a split-log bench outside the open doorway, humid haze and distant water, no people.

beats.vo: Most of the houses held groups of soldiers, not families. There were twenty-six soldiers' wives in the founding party of eight hundred. Most of the cooks were Indian women, or mestizas. The town was a military post, never a colony.
beats.cap: A military post, never a colony
beats.img: A dim interior of a small one-room wattle-and-daub settler house at dusk, a low wood cot along one wall, a clay chamber pot on the packed earth floor, a small plain wooden cross on the opposite wall, a single shaft of low light from a small unglazed window, no people.

beats.vo: Soldiers practiced whatever side trade they could. Francisco Camacho was a soldier and a fisherman. Miguél de Escudón was a soldier and a carpenter. The widow Francisca de Vera rented rooms to five soldiers to keep her household alive.
beats.img: A flat-lay still life on a board floor of a Spanish colonial soldier's side-trade goods: a heavy black iron matchlock musket, a coils of fishing line and a hand-forged iron fishhook, a small wood plane and a hand auger, dim side light, quiet, no people.

beats.vo: Fifty Africans, free and enslaved, landed with Menéndez in fifteen sixty-five. They worked on the early fortifications, sawed timber, and built several structures, including a church, a blacksmith shop, and an artillery platform. The first recorded African-American birth in St. Augustine was in fifteen ninety-five.

card.a_lab: Africans, free and enslaved, in the 1565 founding party

beats.vo: The hospital of La Soledad, established in fifteen ninety-seven, was described in sixteen-oh-five as a miserable hole: a six-bed ward, no doctor in regular attendance. A French barber-surgeon shipwrecked in fifteen seventy-nine had become the town's doctor.
beats.img: A dim small ward at dusk with six low cots in two rows along a packed-earth floor, a single vial of dark medicine and a small cupping glass on a board tray by the door, a small high unglazed window letting in faint grey daylight, muted and quiet, no people.

beats.vo: If God, our Lord, had not sent him to this garrison, men would die like animals. That was the governor's reply when the shipwrecked French barber-surgeon petitioned him for a raise — agreeing, in sixteen-oh-five, that the garrison could not live without him.

card.quote: If God, our Lord, had not sent him to this garrison, men would die like animals.
card.attribution: Governor of Florida · reply to Juan LeConte's petition · c. 1605

beats.vo: In fifteen eighty-six, Francis Drake burned the whole town and fort to the ground. In March of fifteen ninety-nine, a fire swept the wood-and-thatch rebuild. In September, a hurricane flooded what was left. In seventeen-oh-two, a Carolina governor burned the town again — only the new stone Castillo held; the coquina, the Park Service writes, absorbed the cannon shot and compressed.
beats.img: A close still life in soft hazy dawn of a cluster of charred cedar post stubs standing upright in dark waterlogged ground, faint white ash on the surface around them, humid haze and distant flat water beyond, no people.

beats.vo: And in seventeen sixty-three, when Florida was ceded to the British, most of the Spanish residents left for Cuba. The same museum that calls St. Augustine the oldest continuously occupied European town in the United States also titles the section about that year — on the same page — the Spanish Exodus.

card.head: Oldest continuously occupied European town
card.accent: the page with a section titled 'Spanish Exodus'

beats.vo: What actually survived here was not the walls. It was the site — and the people the colony had come to convert, and the people the colony had brought in chains, and the mestizo children of both, who in time became what is still called a founding.
beats.img: A wide flat view at dusk of a low sandy Florida shoreline under a pale grey sky, a single weathered wooden post standing alone at the high-tide line, distant barrier islands and a faint Atlantic horizon, no people, calm and quiet.

beats.vo: Permanent. The word the Park Service uses. The stone is not. The walls are not. The families, mostly, are not. The place is. The site has been continuously occupied since fifteen sixty-five — by someone, in something, on top of something that keeps burning down.
beats.img: A wide symmetrical aerial view at dusk of a low sandy barrier-island shoreline with a quiet inlet bay, distant Atlantic horizon, small soft dunes and palmetto scrub stretching out under a grey humid sky, calm and quiet and almost empty, no people.

beats.vo: Permanent. Fifteen sixty-five to sixteen seventy-two. By Claude.
